subtopics.title: Equate exponents, same base
subtopics.exposition: An exponential equation is an equation that has the unknown variable in the exponent. The rule for equating exponents holds when the base a satisfies a > 0 and a is not equal to 1. If a^x = a^y (same base), then x = y. From the exponent identities, a^0 = 1. If a single term with the same base can be written on each side of an exponential equation, the exponents can be equated; this is one method for solving exponential equations. To solve 3^(x+1) = 9, change the bases to prime numbers by writing 9 as 3^2, so that 3^(x+1) = 3^2. Once the bases are the same, equate the exponents and solve the resulting equation: x + 1 = 2, therefore x = 1. To solve 3^t = 1, write the 1 as a power of the same base using a^0 = 1, so 3^t = 3^0, and equate the exponents to get t = 0.

subtopics.title: Take out common factor
subtopics.exposition: When terms have different exponents of the same base, as in 5^t + 3.5^(t+1) = 400, first rewrite the term with the different exponent: 5^(t+1) is written as 5^t . 5. Take out the common factor 5^t, giving 5^t(1 + 3.5) = 400, which becomes 5^t(1 + 15) = 400. Simplify the bracket and the equation to leave a single power: 5^t(16) = 400 gives 5^t = 25. Change the bases to prime numbers by writing 25 as 5^2, so 5^t = 5^2, then equate the exponents (same base) to get t = 2.

subtopics.title: Solve by factorising
subtopics.exposition: To solve 3^(2x) - 80.3^x - 81 = 0, factorise the trinomial: (3^x - 81)(3^x + 1) = 0. Solve each factor by setting it equal to zero, giving 3^x = 81 or 3^x = -1. For the remaining factor, write 81 as 3^4 so 3^x = 3^4, then equate the exponents to get x = 4. When an equation such as p - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0 is not yet in factorisable form, notice that (p^(1/2))^2 = p and rewrite it as (p^(1/2))^2 - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0. Factorise the rewritten equation as a trinomial: (p^(1/2) - 9)(p^(1/2) - 4) = 0. Solve each factor to find both roots: set p^(1/2) - 9 = 0 and p^(1/2) - 4 = 0, then square both sides of each (for example (p^(1/2))^2 = 9^2) to get p = 81 or p = 16. Both roots are the solution: p = 81 or p = 16. To solve 2^x - 2^(4-x) = 0, first rewrite the equation into a form that can be factorised: 2^(4-x) = 2^4 . 2^(-x) = 2^4 / 2^x. Eliminate the fraction by multiplying both sides of the equation by the denominator, 2^x, which gives 2^(2x) - 16 = 0. The rearranged equation 2^(2x) - 16 = 0 is a difference of two squares and factorises as (2^x - 4)(2^x + 4) = 0.

claims.claim: An exponential equation is an equation that has the unknown variable in the exponent.
If a single term with the same base can be written on each side of an exponential equation, the exponents can be equated; this is one method for solving exponential equations.
The rule for equating exponents holds when the base a satisfies a > 0 and a is not equal to 1.
If a^x = a^y (same base), then x = y.
If the base a = 1, then x and y can be different, so the exponents cannot be equated.
To solve 3^(x+1) = 9, change the bases to prime numbers by writing 9 as 3^2, so that 3^(x+1) = 3^2.
Once the bases are the same, equate the exponents and solve the resulting equation: x + 1 = 2, therefore x = 1.
From the exponent identities, a^0 = 1.
To solve 3^t = 1, write the 1 as a power of the same base using a^0 = 1, so 3^t = 3^0, and equate the exponents to get t = 0.
When terms have different exponents of the same base, as in 5^t + 3.5^(t+1) = 400, first rewrite the term with the different exponent: 5^(t+1) is written as 5^t . 5.
Take out the common factor 5^t, giving 5^t(1 + 3.5) = 400, which becomes 5^t(1 + 15) = 400.
Simplify the bracket and the equation to leave a single power: 5^t(16) = 400 gives 5^t = 25.
Change the bases to prime numbers by writing 25 as 5^2, so 5^t = 5^2, then equate the exponents (same base) to get t = 2.
To solve 3^(2x) - 80.3^x - 81 = 0, factorise the trinomial: (3^x - 81)(3^x + 1) = 0.
Solve each factor by setting it equal to zero, giving 3^x = 81 or 3^x = -1.
3^x = -1 is undefined, so that factor is rejected and only 3^x = 81 is kept.
For the remaining factor, write 81 as 3^4 so 3^x = 3^4, then equate the exponents to get x = 4.
When an equation such as p - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0 is not yet in factorisable form, notice that (p^(1/2))^2 = p and rewrite it as (p^(1/2))^2 - 13p^(1/2) + 36 = 0.
Factorise the rewritten equation as a trinomial: (p^(1/2) - 9)(p^(1/2) - 4) = 0.
Solve each factor to find both roots: set p^(1/2) - 9 = 0 and p^(1/2) - 4 = 0, then square both sides of each (for example (p^(1/2))^2 = 9^2) to get p = 81 or p = 16.
Both roots are the solution: p = 81 or p = 16.
To solve 2^x - 2^(4-x) = 0, first rewrite the equation into a form that can be factorised: 2^(4-x) = 2^4 . 2^(-x) = 2^4 / 2^x.
Eliminate the fraction by multiplying both sides of the equation by the denominator, 2^x, which gives 2^(2x) - 16 = 0.
The rearranged equation 2^(2x) - 16 = 0 is a difference of two squares and factorises as (2^x - 4)(2^x + 4) = 0.
2^x = -4 is rejected because a positive integer with an exponent is always positive; only 2^x = 4 = 2^2 is kept, so x = 2.
